wine.name: Malterdinger Bienenberg Spätburgunder GG
wine.classification: VDP.Grosses Gewächs from the Bienenberg, a VDP.Grosse Lage of Malterdingen
wine.grapes: Spätburgunder alone, the grape known elsewhere as Pinot Noir.
wine.sites: The Bienenberg above Malterdingen, where by the VDP's account Cistercian monks grew Spätburgunder in the fourteenth century: slopes of 20 to 40 per cent at about 200 to 280 metres, facing south to south west, on weathered shell limestone with loess.
wine.making: Picked by hand. The house ferments in part with whole bunches where the year allows, and by importers' sheets for several vintages the wine is then raised for about a year and a half in French barriques, a share of them new, before it is bottled dry.
wine.glass: Red cherry, raspberry and wild strawberry with clove and a peppery, stemmy lift from the whole bunches; light to medium in body, with fine, chalky tannin and fresh acidity carrying a long, cool finish.
wine.ageing: Taut and marked by its barrel for the first few years, it opens after five or so and keeps well beyond a decade in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a wide Burgundy glass.

records.table: Bernhard Huber's Malterdinger Bienenberg Spätburgunder GG is Pinot Noir from shell limestone above Malterdingen in the Breisgau, made in part with whole bunches and raised in French barriques. Look for red cherry, clove and a fine, chalky tannin.
records.story: Cistercian monks from Burgundy, by the VDP's account, were growing Spätburgunder on the Bienenberg at Malterdingen, in the Breisgau north of Freiburg, in the fourteenth century. The Huber family delivered its grapes to the local cooperative until 1987, when the founder, Bernhard Huber, left it and began to bottle and sell the family's wine under his own name. He made his Spätburgunder in the manner of Burgundy: whole bunches where the year allowed, French barriques and a dry finish. The estate grew on the limestone around Malterdingen, Hecklingen, Bombach and Köndringen, and the VDP came to rank the Bienenberg a Grosse Lage. Within the Bienenberg the house singled out Wildenstein, a steep parcel of red shell limestone, sold for years as a Reserve; the VDP came to rank it, provisionally, a Grosse Lage of its own, and its wine became a second Grosses Gewächs. The founder died of illness in June 2014, at fifty five, and his son took the estate on with his mother. The Bienenberg GG shows German Pinot Noir from limestone with the cut and perfume of Burgundy, and makes Malterdingen a name to know.

wine.classification: VDP.Grosses Gewächs from Winklerberg Wanne, a VDP.Grosse Lage of Ihringen
wine.grapes: Spätburgunder alone, the German name for Pinot Noir.
wine.sites: Häusleboden, a parcel in the Wanne of the Winklerberg at Ihringen, named for the family's vineyard hut: near level ground at about 260 metres facing south west, on volcanic rock streaked with lime under a little loess, with vines of the founder's son's selection.
wine.making: Picked by hand from old vines that, by the house's account, give low yields of their own accord. By the sheet of the 2020 vintage the wine was then raised for about a year in barriques and some months more in steel tank before it was bottled dry.
wine.glass: Black and sour cherry, cranberry and cherry stone with bay leaf, violet and a smoky, stony grip; firm and compact in youth, with fine tannin and a tactile, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Tight and marked by new oak on release, it wants five years or more and keeps well beyond a decade in a strong vintage.

records.table: Volcanic rock in the Wanne of the Winklerberg, on the Kaiserstuhl, and old vines the founder's son planted give Dr. Heger's Ihringer Winklerberg Häusleboden Spätburgunder GG its dark cherry, bay leaf and smoke over firm, fine tannin. Give a young bottle an hour of air.
records.story: Ihringen sits at the south west foot of the Kaiserstuhl, the extinct volcano that is the warmest corner of Baden. In 1813, by the VDP's account, a physician of Ihringen bought part of a disused quarry in the Wanne of the Winklerberg and planted vines there. More than a century later another doctor followed him onto the hill. In 1935, as the house tells it, a country doctor of Ihringen, the Dr. Heger of the label, whose patients were mostly growers, began to make wine in his spare time and bought plots on the Ihringer Winklerberg and the Achkarrer Schlossberg. In 1949 he handed the estate to his son, who built it up through the 1960s and, by the house's account, planted the Spätburgunder selection of the Häusleboden. The third generation took on the cellar from 1981, founded the Weinhaus Heger as a second label in 1986, the year the estate joined the VDP, and took over the whole estate in 1992. The family's little vineyard hut in the Wanne gave the Häusleboden its name. Taste it for what volcanic rock makes of Spätburgunder.

wine.name: Achkarrer Schlossberg Grauburgunder GG
wine.classification: VDP.Grosses Gewächs from the Schlossberg, a VDP.Grosse Lage of Achkarren
wine.grapes: Grauburgunder alone, the grape known in France as Pinot Gris.
wine.sites: The Schlossberg north of Achkarren on the Kaiserstuhl: a steep slope of 20 to 60 per cent, between about 200 and 310 metres, facing south west to south east, on stony volcanic soil.
wine.making: Pressed gently and fermented in stainless steel. By the sheets for the 2020 and 2021 vintages the wine then spends about a year in large oak casks and six months more on its full lees in steel tank before it is bottled dry.
wine.glass: Ripe pear, quince and yellow apple with a smoky, flinty note and a touch of hazelnut from the large casks; full and broad yet dry, held by firm acidity and a salty, stony finish.
wine.ageing: Open on release, it gains nut, honey and smoke over five to eight years and keeps for a decade in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle briefly; a large white wine glass.

records.table: Made with a meal in mind, Franz Keller's Achkarrer Schlossberg Grauburgunder GG is dry Pinot Gris from a steep volcanic slope of the Kaiserstuhl. After a year in large oak casks it shows pear, quince and smoke over firm acidity.
records.story: In Oberbergen, in the heart of the Kaiserstuhl, the Keller family's story runs through the Schwarzer Adler, the village inn. By the VDP's account a wine business grew up around the inn at the turn of the twentieth century, and the estate came to carry the name of Franz Keller (1927 to 2007), the father of the present head. In 1969, as the house tells it, the family's kitchen at the Schwarzer Adler won its first Michelin star, so the wines have long been made with a meal in mind; the house says it takes its lead from the dry wines and the way of life of its French neighbours across the Rhine. When land consolidation reshaped the Kaiserstuhl into broad terraces in the early 1970s, Franz Keller fought it, by the house's account, to keep small plots and steep slopes. In the 1980s the family dug the Bergkeller, cellars that reach some 112 metres into the loess. The estate joined the VDP in 2014, and the Schlossberg at Achkarren, a steep volcanic hill, gives its Grauburgunder Grosses Gewächs. When a guest asks what the white Pinot of Baden can be beside food, open this one.

traps: The Schwarzer Adler is the family's restaurant and hotel at Oberbergen, not a wine or a vineyard.
Hecklingen in the Breisgau has a Schlossberg too, a Grosse Lage of Bernhard Huber; read the village before the site.
Grauburgunder is Pinot Gris made dry; Weissburgunder is Pinot Blanc and Spätburgunder is Pinot Noir.

The Michelin star of 1969 rests on the house and the VDP; the claim that it has been held without a break was left out as volatile. The Bergkeller of the 1980s and the stand against the land consolidation are the house's own account, hedged.

The élevage rests on two sellers' sheets (2020 and 2021); no source confirms a wild fermentation, so none is claimed. The label prints Schlossberg Achkarren or Achkarren Schlossberg; the plan's Achkarrer form is kept in the name as the lint asks.

wine.name: Neuweierer Mauerberg Riesling GG
wine.classification: VDP.Grosses Gewächs from Mauerberg Mauerwein, a VDP.Grosse Lage of Neuweier
wine.sites: The Mauerberg above Neuweier, in the hills south of Baden-Baden: an exposed slope of up to about 60 per cent by the estate's account, facing between south and west south west, on arkose, a sandstone rich in feldspar and quartz.
wine.making: Picked by hand on the steep slope, pressed, fermented dry and bottled in the Bocksbeutel. Accounts of the cellar differ, steel tank in one and a share of wood with wild yeasts in a seller's sheet for 2021, so no single vessel is claimed here.
wine.glass: Yellow peach, lime zest and elderflower over a smoky, stony note, with a savoury depth; dry and firm, with ripe acidity and a long, salty finish.
wine.ageing: Firm on release, it opens after three to five years and keeps for a decade and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass.

label.means: The name of the Grosse Lage within the Mauerberg, which labels print beside the site's own name.
The village in the Rebland of Baden-Baden and its steep Riesling slope.
GG: a dry wine of the VDP from a vineyard it ranks Grosse Lage.

records.table: The flat Bocksbeutel, Franken's flask, which Neuweier may use by an old right, holds Schloss Neuweier's Mauerberg Riesling GG, a dry Riesling from a steep slope by Baden-Baden. Peach, lime and smoke run over firm acidity.
records.story: Neuweier lies in the Rebland, the wine villages in the hills south of Baden-Baden, and its castle goes back to the Middle Ages. In 1785, as local accounts tell it, the castle's lord had Riesling planted in his vineyards, vines brought from Nierstein and Laubenheim, and the quality of the valley's wine rose with them. By the early nineteenth century the wine of the Mauerberg was going into the Bocksbeutel, the flat, round flask otherwise kept for Franken. One account says the lord brought the bottle from his Franconian home, another that a bishop of Würzburg granted the right in the eighteenth century; either way Neuweier and a few neighbouring villages of the Rebland are among the few places outside Franken that may use it, and the Mauerberg Riesling is the wine that carries that right into a dining room. In 2012 the castle estate was sold to a new family. The VDP ranks two of the estate's slopes as Grosse Lagen, the Mauerberg Mauerwein and the neighbouring Goldenes Loch, both planted to Riesling. Two lessons travel in it: that Baden, a land of Pinot, grows serious Riesling in the Ortenau, and that the shape of a bottle can be a legal right.

traps: The Bocksbeutel is not only Franken's: Neuweier and a few neighbouring villages of the Rebland in Baden may use it too.
Mauerwein is the Grosse Lage within the Mauerberg; a Neuweierer Mauerberg Riesling of Erste Lage rank is a different wine.
Schloss Neuweier is in the Ortenau by Baden-Baden, not on the Kaiserstuhl, and its flagship is Riesling, not Pinot.

report: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. The VDP lists the estate under a name that carries its living owner's name; the record uses the plan's Schloss Neuweier and avoids that page's address. The owner (Robert Schätzle) and an earlier figure of the estate (Gisela Joos), both of unsettled status, are names for people.json.

The planting of 1785 with vines from Nierstein and Laubenheim rests on wein.plus and the town's tourism page. The plan gives the lord as Baron Philipp Franz von Knebel-Katzenellenbogen (1733 to 1816); wein.plus gives that name and those dates, the tourism page gives Philipp Knebel of Katzenellenbogen without dates, and a search for the dates found no second source, so the story says the castle's lord.

The Bocksbeutel: wein.plus says the Mauerberg's wine went into it by the early nineteenth century and the right still holds; the tourism page names Neuweier, Steinbach and Varnhalt and says a bishop of Würzburg granted it in the eighteenth century, while the same page credits the lord with bringing the bottle from Würzburg; the story gives both accounts.

Site: the estate gives up to 60 per cent and an exposed south slope, the VDP west south west and Carboniferous rock; the estate's VDP page gives arkose sandstone rich in feldspar and quartz; wein.plus gives porphyry, granite and loess, not used.

The making rests on one seller's sheet for 2021 (long pressing, two days' settling, wild yeasts, part in wood); wein.plus says the estate's Rieslings are raised in steel. The record hedges to one vintage; a checker should confirm or cut.

The sale of 2012 rests on wein.plus and trade accounts; the age of the castle (twelfth or thirteenth century) differs between sources, so the story says the Middle Ages. Falstaff prints the wine as Mauerwein Neuweier Mauerberg Riesling GG; the plan's form is kept as the lint asks.

changed: wine.sites: the soil is now arkose, a sandstone rich in feldspar and quartz, as the estate gives it, the slope up to about 60 per cent by the estate and the aspect between south and west south west; the Carboniferous rock was not confirmed and is cut.

wine.making: the seller's sheet of 2021 (long pressing, two days' settling, wild yeasts, part in wood) is one source against wein.plus's steel; the field now says accounts differ and claims no vessel.

story, table, traps, questions[0]: 'Neuweier, Steinbach and Varnhalt are the villages outside Franken that may use it' is now 'Neuweier and a few neighbouring villages of the Rebland are among the few places outside Franken': Umweg is named beside them in other accounts and the Tauber valley of northern Baden bottles in the Bocksbeutel too. The lord's bottle now comes 'from his Franconian home', as a Badischer Wein list gives it; was 'his estate at Würzburg'.

questions[0]: the distractor 'A Franken bottle used under licence from Würzburg' was half true (one account has a bishop of Würzburg grant the right) and is now 'A Franken bottle bought in for a single vintage'.
open: The lord of 1785, Baron Philipp Franz von Knebel-Katzenellenbogen (1733 to 1816), stays undescribed by name: his dates rest on wein.plus alone.
The exact list of places outside Franken that may use the Bocksbeutel was not read in the Weinverordnung itself; the record names no closed list.

wine.name: Jaspis 10hoch4 Gutedel
wine.grapes: Gutedel alone, the grape known in Switzerland and France as Chasselas.
wine.sites: Old Gutedel vines, planted around 1970, on limestone at Efringen-Kirchen in the south of the Markgräflerland; Jaspis, German for jasper, marks the house's leading wines, from old vines.
wine.making: Picked by hand and pressed. The must ferments with its own wild yeasts, and by sellers' sheets the wine then rests for about two years on its lees in wooden casks of a few hundred litres before it is bottled dry.
wine.glass: Lemon peel, white pear and fresh hazelnut over a salty, chalky grip, with a faint smoky note from the long time in wood; dense yet moderate in alcohol, with fine phenolic grip and a long, tense finish.
wine.ageing: Taut on release after its long time in cask, it gains depth over five years and more, and a strong vintage keeps for a decade.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for half an hour; a white wine glass.

label.means: The house's mark for its leading wines, from old vines; Jaspis is the German word for jasper.
Ten to the power four, written out; sellers explain the name in different ways.
A country wine category; the house bottles much of its range this way rather than as Qualitätswein.

records.table: Ziereisen's Jaspis 10hoch4 Gutedel is Chasselas taken seriously: old vines on limestone near Basel, wild yeasts and about two years on the lees in wooden casks. It is moderate in alcohol yet dense, with pear, hazelnut and a salty finish.
records.story: The Markgräflerland, the southern tip of Baden between Freiburg and Basel, is the German home of Gutedel, the grape Switzerland calls Chasselas. Ziereisen is a young estate at Efringen-Kirchen, founded by a couple of the village in 1991 or 1992, for the sources differ, and it took another road. It does not belong to the VDP, and it bottles much of its range as Landwein, the plain country wine category, rather than under the region's Qualitätswein names, so a guest who reads Landwein on the label should not take it for a lesser wine. Its leading wines, from old vines, carry the word Jaspis, German for the stone jasper; some of its vines, planted for Spätburgunder, go back to 1958. The Gutedel called 10hoch4 comes from vines planted around 1970 on limestone, ferments with its own yeasts and then rests for about two years on its lees in wooden casks of a few hundred litres. Earlier labels print it as Jaspis 10hoch4 Gutedel, later ones as 10hoch4 Gutedel. It shows what Chasselas can become with old vines, limestone and time in cask, and that a German category on a label need not measure the wine.

traps: Landwein on a Ziereisen label is the house's choice of category, not a sign of a lesser wine.
Gutedel is Chasselas, the grape of the Swiss Vaud, not a crossing and not Silvaner.
Jaspis 10hoch4 Gutedel and 10hoch4 Gutedel are one wine under an earlier and a later label.

report: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS, and no primary source was reached: the house's own site did not come up, so every fact rests on two secondary sources. The founder and his wife are living and are not named; Falstaff's addresses carry the founder's name, so none is cited. Names for people.json: Hanspeter Ziereisen, Edeltraud Ziereisen.
Founded is empty: two sellers give 1991, wein.plus gives 1992, and the story says so.

The meaning of 10hoch4 is unsettled: one seller gives 10,000 vines a hectare, Vinum 11,000 and says the name alludes to the density, another seller the yeast cells in a millilitre; the record says only that sellers explain it differently. The plan's guess of a planting density is not confirmed.

The vines of around 1970 rest on Vinum (planted 1968) and Skurnik (around 1970); the 1958 vines are Skurnik's for the Zipsin Pinot Noir and vinoscout's 1958 to 1962 for the Jaspis vines. The élevage is 22 months in 650 litre casks by one seller's sheet and 24 months in wood by Falstaff, so the record says about two years.

Why the house bottles as Landwein was not found in any source; the record says only that it does. The label category also appears as Badischer Landwein and, later, Landwein Oberrhein; the appellation field says Landwein, Baden.
The house leads with Gutedel in the sources read; the pick stands. Left out: the Gault and Millau mark of 2015 (a score) and the site name of the 10hoch4 vineyard, which no source gave.

changed: wine.sites, wine.label[0], story: Jaspis now marks the house's leading wines, from old vines, and is German for jasper; was 'from its oldest vines' and 'a gemstone prized for its rarity', a seller's line, with 'oldest' a claim of rank unsourced.

wine.making, story, cards[1]: the casks are now 'of a few hundred litres'; one seller gives 650 litres and Falstaff 500 litres for 2016, so no size is claimed. 'Unfiltered' was cut: the only source found says it of the house's Grauburgunder.
wine.glass, table: 'light in alcohol' is now 'moderate in alcohol': Falstaff gives 10.5 per cent for 2021 and 12 for 2016 and 2018.
open: The meaning of 10hoch4 is still unsettled, as the author reported.
